lead: A straight column under axial compression is in equilibrium when it stays straight. That equilibrium is stable only up to a load of π²EI/L<sub>e</sub>². At that load a tiny sideways bow grows instead of shrinking: the column buckles. The idea matters because a thin tube can carry far less than its material's squash load, and aircraft struts, engine-mount tubes and truss-rib members are thin. Euler's formula gives the critical load from stiffness and length alone, so it is the first check on any slender compression member.
prereq: You need: the beam curvature relation EI d²v/dx² = M, and the idea of a strut as a two-force member in a truss.

blocks.text: Take a straight column of length L, area A and second moment of area I. Push it with an axial load P. If a small sideways deflection v(x) appears, the load line is no longer over the centroid of the section. The load then makes a bending moment M = P v at that section. The column's bending stiffness resists it, and for small slopes the curvature is v'' = d²v/dx². Equilibrium of the slice gives EI v'' = −P v.

blocks.where: E is Young's modulus in Pa; I is the second moment of area about the bending axis in m⁴; v is the lateral deflection in m; x is distance along the column in m; P is the axial compression in N.

items: Pinned ends give v = 0 at x = 0 and x = L.
Set k² = P/(EI). Then v'' + k²v = 0.
Solution v = C₁ sin kx + C₂ cos kx, where C₁ and C₂ are constants; v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = 0.
v(L) = 0 gives C₁ sin kL = 0. C₁ = 0 is the straight column; a bent shape needs sin kL = 0, and the first buckle is kL = π.

blocks.text: The formula is Euler's critical load. It is also called Euler’s theory of struts. It contains no strength term: a stronger alloy with the same E and I buckles at the same load.

items: Perfectly straight: an initial bow adds bending at once; see imperfections and eccentric loading.
Elastic: P/A must stay below the proportional limit; otherwise use inelastic buckling.
Centroidal load: an offset e adds a moment P e.
Small deflection: curvature is close to v''.
Ends hold position but allow the assumed rotation.

blocks.text: End fixity decides how much of the column can bend. A pinned end allows rotation but holds position. A fixed end allows neither. The effective length L<sub>e</sub> is the length of an equivalent pinned-pinned column with the same P<sub>cr</sub>. The factor K multiplies the real length: L<sub>e</sub> = K L, where K has no unit and L is in m.

blocks.where: P<sub>cr</sub> is the Euler buckling load in N; K is the effective-length factor; L is the real column length in m.

blocks.text: Fixed-free is the weakest because the free tip can move sideways with no support. Fixed-fixed is the strongest: the buckled shape is a full cosine wave over L, and its middle half, between the points of contraflexure at L/4 and 3L/4, is a pinned half-wave of length L/2, so Le = 0.5L. Real joints sit between these ideals. A riveted tube end is closer to fixed; a single pin is closer to pinned. When the same member also carries bending, see beam-columns.

Slenderness measures how thin a column is. The radius of gyration is r = √(I/A), in m, where A is the cross-section area in m². Slenderness is λ = L<sub>e</sub>/r, dimensionless. A stocky column has small λ; a slender one has large λ.

blocks.where: λ is the slenderness ratio; L<sub>e</sub> is the effective length in m; r is the radius of gyration in m; I is the second moment of area in m⁴; A is the area in m².

blocks.text: Euler's formula is valid while the buckling stress Pcr/A is below the proportional limit. Setting π²E/λ² equal to the proportional limit σprop gives the limiting slenderness √(π²E/σprop): about 99 for mild steel (E = 200 GPa, σprop ≈ 200 MPa) and about 59 for an aluminium alloy (E = 70 GPa, σprop ≈ 200 MPa). Euler needs λ above that value. Below that, the column fails by yielding or by inelastic buckling, covered in Rankine-Gordon formula for intermediate columns and inelastic buckling.

A column buckles about the axis with the smallest I. For a rectangle, I = b h³/12 about the centroidal axis parallel to b. If h > b, the smaller I is about the other axis, so the column bows in the direction of the smaller dimension. Always compare I about both centroidal axes and use the smaller value.

In aircraft, engine-mount tubes and truss-rib struts are slender compression members. Their ends are often flattened and bolted, which gives partial fixity. A dent or a loose fitting can reduce the load below Euler's value. Local ovalisation or wall buckling can also happen first; that is a plate-buckling check, made separately.

figure.caption: The 2 m aluminium strut of the worked example (EI = 1.4 × 10⁴ N·m², A = 500 mm²) under four end conditions, with its first buckled shape. Free-ended it carries only 8.6 kN because L<sub>e</sub> = 4 m. Fixed at both ends Euler gives 138.2 kN, but that is 276 MPa, past the proportional limit, so the real strut fails earlier.

spec.aria: Four vertical struts, each with an axial load P on top and its buckled shape: pinned-pinned, a half sine wave, P critical 34.5 kilonewtons; fixed-fixed, a full cosine wave, 138.2 kilonewtons marked not valid; fixed-pinned, 70.5 kilonewtons; fixed-free, a quarter wave with the tip swinging out, 8.6 kilonewtons. Each is labelled with its K factor and effective length.

examples.question: An aluminium strut has E = 70 GPa, length L = 2.0 m, I = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m⁴ and A = 500 mm². It is pinned at both ends. (a) Find the Euler buckling load and the slenderness ratio. (b) Find the mean stress at buckling and state whether the elastic formula is valid if the alloy's proportional limit is about 200 MPa. (c) Repeat the buckling load for fixed-fixed, fixed-pinned and fixed-free ends.
steps: Convert: E = 70×10⁹ Pa, I = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m⁴, A = 500 mm² = 5.0×10⁻⁴ m², L = 2.0 m.
Pinned ends: K = 1.0, so L<sub>e</sub> = 2.0 m.
σ = P<sub>cr</sub>/A = 34 543.6 / 5.0×10⁻⁴ = 6.909×10⁷ Pa = 69.1 MPa. This is below 200 MPa, so the elastic formula is valid.

Fixed-fixed: K = 0.5, so P<sub>cr</sub> = 34.5436/0.5² = 138.2 kN. Its mean stress would be 138 200/5.0×10⁻⁴ = 276 MPa, above the 200 MPa proportional limit, so this Euler value is not valid: the fixed-fixed strut fails inelastically at a lower load.
Fixed-pinned: K = 0.7, so P<sub>cr</sub> = 34.5436/0.7² = 70.5 kN, a mean stress of 141 MPa, below 200 MPa, so Euler is valid.
examples.answer: Pinned: P<sub>cr</sub> = 34.5 kN, r = 20.0 mm, λ = 100.0, σ = 69.1 MPa (Euler valid); fixed-pinned 70.5 kN (valid, 141 MPa); fixed-free 8.6 kN; fixed-fixed 138.2 kN by Euler, but at 276 MPa that is above the proportional limit, so the real fixed-fixed strut fails below it.
examples.check:
import math
E = 70e9
L = 2.0
I = 2.0e-7
A = 5.0e-4
P = math.pi**2 * E * I / L**2
print(round(P / 1000, 1))
r = math.sqrt(I / A)
print(round(r * 1000, 1))
print(round(L / r, 1))
print(round(P / A / 1e6, 1))
for K in (0.5, 0.7, 2.0):
    print(round(P / K**2 / 1000, 1))

traps: Using the full length L in π²EI/L² for a fixed or fixed-free strut. Replace L by L<sub>e</sub> = K L before squaring.
Taking I about the stronger axis. The column bows about the axis with the smaller I, so use I<sub>min</sub>.
Mixing units: E in GPa, I in mm⁴ and L in m. Convert everything to N and m before substituting.
Thinking P<sub>cr</sub> depends on yield strength. Euler's load depends on E and I, not on the yield stress; yield only decides whether the elastic formula is allowed.
Using Euler for a stocky column where P<sub>cr</sub>/A is above the proportional limit. Use the Rankine-Gordon formula or the tangent-modulus method there.

quiz.q: State Euler's buckling formula for a pinned-pinned column and define each symbol.
quiz.a: P<sub>cr</sub> = π²EI/L², where E is Young's modulus in Pa, I is the second moment of area in m⁴, and L is the column length in m.

quiz.q: Why does a perfect straight column buckle at a load that depends on stiffness and length, not on yield strength?
quiz.a: A perfect column has no bending until a small sideways deflection appears. At P<sub>cr</sub> the deflected shape satisfies equilibrium with no extra lateral load. Yield matters only after P/A reaches the proportional limit; below that, buckling is a stiffness phenomenon.

quiz.q: A steel strut has E = 200 GPa, I = 1.0×10⁻⁷ m⁴, L = 1.5 m and is fixed at one end and free at the other. Find its Euler buckling load.
quiz.a: Fixed-free: K = 2.0, so L<sub>e</sub> = 3.0 m. P<sub>cr</sub> = π² × 200×10⁹ × 1.0×10⁻⁷ / 3.0² = 21 932 N ≈ 21.9 kN.

quiz.q: A strut is pinned in one plane and fixed in the other. Which plane buckles first?
quiz.a: Pinned plane: K = 1.0, P = π²EI/L². Fixed plane: K = 0.5, P = 4π²EI/L² for the same I. The pinned plane buckles first unless its I is more than four times the I in the fixed plane.

quiz.q: Why is the effective-length factor for a fixed-free column equal to 2.0?
quiz.a: The free tip can translate. The buckled shape is a quarter sine wave over L. Mirror it to make a half sine wave of length 2L between two pins, so L<sub>e</sub> = 2L.

quiz.q: A pinned strut has A = 600 mm², I = 3.0×10⁻⁷ m⁴ and L = 1.8 m. Find the radius of gyration and the slenderness ratio.
List the four standard end conditions with their effective-length factors.
quiz.a: Pinned-pinned K = 1.0; fixed-fixed K = 0.5; fixed-pinned K = 0.7; fixed-free K = 2.0.

quiz.q: Why is Euler's formula unsafe for a short aluminium tube with λ = 40?
quiz.a: At λ = 40 the Euler stress P<sub>cr</sub>/A is above the proportional limit. The tube yields or buckles inelastically before the Euler load, so Euler overestimates the strength. Use the Rankine-Gordon formula or the tangent-modulus method.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry checks strut stability with finite-element eigenvalue buckling, then knocks the load down for imperfections and joint play. Search for “effective length factor” and “eigenvalue buckling”.
